x.A: Multi-AZ gives high availability, but its standby doesn't serve traffic, so it doesn't improve read and write performance.
x.B: OpenSearch Service is a search and analytics engine, and moving to it is a big change and not designed for rapid updates of transactional location data.
x.C: DAX is a cache for DynamoDB only and can't sit in front of an RDS for PostgreSQL database.
x.D: ElastiCache for Redis handles rapid reads and writes of location data in memory, and it has geospatial commands, so it takes the load off the database and improves performance.

x.A: A Lambda function that restores deleted tables after the fact still leaves downtime and needs custom code.
x.B: A backup and restore plan with manual recovery means the table is still deleted, with downtime until someone restores it.
x.C: Deletion protection prevents a table from being deleted by accident, so there is no disruption in the first place. It's one setting, so it takes the least overhead.
x.D: Point-in-time recovery restores data after deletion, but doesn't prevent the deletion, so there would still be disruption.

x.A: Glacier with expedited retrieval has retrieval fees and delays, so it isn't immediate retrieval at no additional cost.
x.B: Cached volumes store data in S3 and keep frequently accessed data locally, which frees on-premises capacity, minimizes bandwidth, and gives immediate access to hot data at no retrieval cost.
x.C: Stored volumes keep all the data locally, so the on-premises storage capacity problem isn't solved.
x.D: Direct Connect adds cost and keeping all data locally doesn't solve the capacity problem.

x.A: Step scaling on CPU is reactive only, and doesn't use historical trends to forecast.
x.B: Predictive scaling forecasts load from daily and weekly history and scales ahead of time, and dynamic scaling with target tracking handles live changes in utilization. Together they meet both needs.
x.C: A scheduled action is based on fixed times and doesn't adapt to live changes or analyze each resource's trends.
x.D: A simple scaling policy with a longer cooldown is reactive and doesn't forecast.

x.A: ElastiCache for Redis caches the repeated read results of delivery details, so the database isn't hit by the same queries again and again. It reduces the load for less cost than more database capacity.
x.B: Another read replica helps only for a while, and the repeated reads would continue to grow the load, with higher cost.
x.C: Aurora Auto Scaling adds replicas as load rises, which costs more and still runs the repeated queries on the database.
x.D: Aurora MySQL multi-master (multiple writers) is for write scaling, and the problem is repeated reads.

x.A: DynamoDB doesn't have read replicas that you add to a table.
x.B: A GSI gives another way to query the data, but it doesn't change the consistency of reads, and GSI reads are only eventually consistent.
x.C: DynamoDB reads are eventually consistent by default. Requesting strongly consistent reads returns the latest data.
x.D: Eventually consistent reads are what the application is already getting, so they would keep returning stale data.

x.A: Security groups and network ACLs filter by IP and port and can't detect SQL injection in web requests.
x.B: AWS WAF blocks SQL injection and other web attacks against the application, and RDS parameter groups configure database security settings. It needs little overhead.
x.C: Network Firewall inspects network traffic, but it's more to deploy and manage than WAF, and isn't what you'd use to protect an RDS database.
x.D: Using least-privileged database accounts is good, but the company has done it already, and it doesn't protect the application from web attacks.

x.A: SCPs set permission boundaries and can't identify failed login attempts to a database.
x.B: GuardDuty RDS Protection analyzes login activity to Aurora databases and finds abnormal failed and incomplete login attempts, and it can be enabled across the organization's member accounts with little effort.
x.C: Publishing general logs to CloudWatch Logs and exporting them doesn't analyze the data to identify abnormal logins, and it takes more work.
x.D: CloudTrail records API calls, not database login attempts.

x.A: Inter-Region VPC peering connects VPCs but not the on-premises data centers, and many VPCs means many peering connections.
x.B: A private virtual interface connects to VPCs in the same Region (or through a Direct Connect gateway), not directly to VPCs in other Regions.
x.C: A mesh of EC2 VPN appliances with VPN CloudHub is complex to build and run, and isn't scalable.
x.D: A Direct Connect gateway connects Direct Connect connections to virtual private gateways of VPCs in multiple Regions, so both data centers and all VPCs can communicate, with little operational work.

x.A: Kinesis Data Streams handles traffic spikes and keeps records in order per shard, Lambda processes them without servers, and DynamoDB is a highly available managed database.
x.B: EC2 instances for processing and Redshift for storage mean managing servers and aren't suited to a leaderboard.
x.C: SNS doesn't keep messages in order, and a SQL database on EC2 isn't highly available or managed.
x.D: A standard SQS queue doesn't guarantee order, and EC2 instances with Auto Scaling add servers to manage.

x.A: A lifecycle policy can't copy objects to another bucket. It transitions or expires objects.
x.B: S3 Same-Region Replication copies new logs automatically from each account's bucket into the central bucket within us-west-2, with no code, so logs don't leave the Region and cost stays low.
x.C: A daily script copying the whole contents is a custom job to run and costs more by copying everything repeatedly.
x.D: Lambda functions in every account need code, and invocation costs add up for each object.

x.A: One-way replication from the main bucket to both buckets doesn't replicate uploads made in the other Regions back to the other buckets, so they would be missing.
x.B: Chaining one-way replication means content uploaded in one Region doesn't reach all other buckets, and it adds delay.
x.C: Two-way replication among all three buckets keeps the data in sync no matter which Region a video is uploaded to, so developers upload near them and students stream near them.
x.D: A Multi-Region Access Point for streaming only leaves uploads going to one Region, so developers far from it still have high latency.
x.E: A Multi-Region Access Point gives a single global endpoint that routes both uploads and streaming to the closest bucket, so latency is minimized, and the application only changes the endpoint.

x.A: CloudFront is mainly for downloads, and using it for uploads to a single bucket doesn't give the lowest latency in the user's Region.
x.B: Transfer Acceleration speeds uploads over long distances to one bucket, but the content is consumed mostly in the Region where it's uploaded, so it adds cost and a longer path than a local bucket.
x.C: Uploading to EC2 instances and copying to S3 adds servers and an extra hop.
x.D: Uploading to the S3 bucket in the Region closest to the user gives the lowest upload latency, and CloudFront distributions deliver the content quickly where it's consumed.

x.A: SNS with SQS queues provides filtering, but requires many queues and polling configuration, which is more overhead.
x.B: EventBridge receives events from API Gateway, and rules with event patterns filter messages so each target Lambda function receives only what it needs. It's a managed service with little configuration.
x.C: MSK is a Kafka cluster that you would manage, and it doesn't publish messages to Lambda functions with filtering in a simple way.
x.D: Sending to several SQS queues requires the API to know about each queue, and no message filtering is built in.

x.A: S3 Inventory lists unencrypted objects, S3 Batch Operations re-encrypts them with SSE-C by copying, and default encryption applies to future objects. This covers existing and future data with the customer-provided key.
x.B: SSE-KMS uses KMS keys, not a customer-provided key, and Storage Lens doesn't encrypt anything.
x.C: AWS Batch isn't how you encrypt S3 objects, and SSE-KMS isn't the customer-provided key required.
x.D: The usage report can't list unencrypted objects, and this doesn't encrypt existing objects.

x.A: A Route 53 public hosted zone for the domain with the existing zone file imported moves DNS hosting quickly to a highly available managed service.
x.B: A private hosted zone resolves names only within VPCs, so it can't serve the public website.
x.C: Simple AD and zone transfers aren't how you migrate public DNS hosting, and it adds servers to manage.
x.D: A Resolver inbound endpoint is for forwarding queries from on-premises networks to VPCs, so it doesn't move the DNS hosting to AWS.

x.A: AppConfig manages application configuration, and Secrets Manager stores and retrieves credentials securely with rotation. Both are managed, so the overhead is the least.
x.B: Lambda isn't a place to store configuration, and Parameter Store lacks automatic rotation for credentials.
x.C: Files in S3 need code to encrypt, fetch, and manage them, and there's no rotation.
x.D: RDS isn't a place to store credentials for the application, because credentials are needed to reach it in the first place.

x.A: IAM database authentication handles authentication, not encryption of the data in transit.
x.B: Self-signed certificates are not trusted by default, and it isn't how you secure RDS connections.
x.C: Restoring with encryption turns on encryption at rest, which is already enabled, and doesn't encrypt data in transit.
x.D: RDS supports SSL/TLS. Downloading the AWS-provided root certificates and using them in client connections encrypts the data in transit.

x.A: An NLB can have a static Elastic IP address for each AZ, so clients can allow those fixed addresses on their firewalls.
x.B: An ALB doesn't support Elastic IP addresses. Its IP addresses can change.
x.C: An A record can point to an Elastic IP, but the question has a load balancer, and EIPs attach to instances or NLBs, not directly to give a load-balanced endpoint.
x.D: A proxy instance is a single point of failure and adds management.

x.A: The root user can't be disabled, so this isn't possible.
x.B: Creating IAM users for daily work and turning on MFA on the root user protects the root account, which should be used only for the few tasks that require it.
x.C: Root access keys shouldn't be created and used for daily work, because it's a major security risk.
x.D: Sharing the root credentials and using root for daily tasks is the opposite of best practice.

x.A: Enhanced networking gives higher bandwidth, higher packets per second, and lower latency between instances.
x.B: Separate accounts have nothing to do with network latency.
x.C: A cluster placement group puts instances close together in one AZ, which gives the lowest latency between nodes.
x.D: Attaching multiple network interfaces doesn't lower latency between nodes.
x.E: EBS optimized instances improve storage throughput, not network latency between nodes.

x.A: Direct Connect is a network link, not a migration tool, and S3 would change how the applications access the data.
x.B: FSx for Lustre is a Linux file system and isn't SMB-based, so applications would need to change.
x.C: DataSync handles millions of small files and preserves the directory structure. FSx for Windows File Server provides SMB file shares, so the applications don't change.
x.D: A volume gateway provides block storage over iSCSI, not SMB file shares.

x.A: CloudWatch cross-account observability lets a monitoring account query and visualize metrics, logs, and traces across accounts. Deploying the provided CloudFormation template in each source account shares the data with it, with little effort.
x.B: SCPs only restrict permissions and don't share CloudWatch data across accounts.
x.C: An IAM user with policies in each account is manual and uses long-term credentials, and it doesn't give a unified view.
x.D: Cross-account IAM policies for a user in the monitoring account is more manual work, and doesn't use the built-in observability feature.

x.A: CloudFront distributions don't have network ACLs, so you can't add a deny rule there.
x.B: AWS WAF already protects the site, and adding an IP match condition (an IP set rule) to block the malicious IP stops it at the edge.
x.C: The instances are behind the ALB, so their network ACLs would see the ALB's address, not the client's IP, and wouldn't block the attacker.
x.D: Security groups can't deny, and they would see the ALB's IP address rather than the client's.

x.A: Creating IAM users for several thousand employees in each account is a lot to manage, and doesn't use a central identity source.
x.B: Root users shouldn't be used for employees, and root credentials can't be synchronized from an IdP.
x.C: IAM Identity Center connects to the existing IdP, and provisions users and groups so employees sign in once and get access to all 10 accounts through permission sets.
x.D: RAM shares resources, not account access for users from an identity provider.
